claims.text: What the image looks like Centrally dilated loops with valvulae conniventes; stepladder air-fluid levels; absent colonic gas → small bowel obstruction (SBO)
claims.quote: Centrally dilated loops with valvulae conniventes; stepladder air-fluid levels; absent colonic gas Small bowel obstruction (SBO)

claims.text: Plain films: a ladderlike series of distended small-bowel loops is typical of SBO but may also occur with obstruction of the right colon; fluid levels show on upright views
claims.quote: On plain radiographs, a ladderlike series of distended small-bowel loops is typical of small-bowel obstruction but may also occur with obstruction of the right colon. Fluid levels in the bowel can be seen in upright views.

claims.text: Buzzword: stepladder air-fluid levels on upright KUB → small bowel obstruction
claims.quote: Stepladder air-fluid levels Upright KUB Small bowel obstruction

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Small bowel: central; valvulae conniventes cross the full lumen; dilated > 3 cm
claims.quote: small bowel = central, valvulae conniventes cross full lumen, dilated >3 cm.

claims.text: Air-fluid levels on upright: > 2.5 cm or stepladder = obstruction
claims.quote: Air-fluid levels on upright (>2.5 cm or stepladder = obstruction).

claims.text: Distended loops and fluid levels may be absent with obstruction of the proximal jejunum or with closed-loop strangulating obstruction (as may occur with volvulus)
claims.quote: Distended loops and fluid levels may be absent with an obstruction of the proximal jejunum or with closed-loop strangulating obstructions (as may occur with volvulus).

claims.text: Ileus can give similar, perhaps less dramatic, films and symptoms; telling them apart can be difficult
claims.quote: Similar, although perhaps less dramatic, radiographic findings and symptoms occur in ileus (paralysis of the intestine without obstruction); differentiation can be difficult.

claims.text: CT: dilated proximal bowel and collapsed distal bowel are highly suggestive; a transition point cannot always be seen
claims.quote: A specific point of obstruction (transition point) cannot always be seen on CT, but the dilated proximal bowel and collapsed distal bowel are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.

claims.text: Causes Most common causes: adhesions, hernias and tumors; SBO without prior surgery or hernias is often caused by a tumor
claims.quote: The most common causes of obstruction are adhesions, hernias, and tumors; a small-bowel obstruction in the absence of prior surgery or hernias is often caused by a tumor.

claims.text: Mechanism: fluid, food, secretions and gas accumulate above the obstruction; the proximal bowel distends and the distal segment collapses
claims.quote: Ingested fluid and food, digestive secretions, and gas accumulate above the obstruction. The proximal bowel distends, and the distal segment collapses.

claims.text: Strangulation (compromised blood flow) occurs in nearly 25% of SBO, usually with hernia, volvulus or intussusception; it can progress to infarction and gangrene in as little as 6 hours
claims.quote: Strangulating obstruction is obstruction with compromised blood flow; it occurs in nearly 25% of patients with small-bowel obstruction (1). It is usually associated with hernia, volvulus, and intussusception. Strangulating obstruction can progress to infarction and gangrene in as little as 6 hours.

claims.text: Symptoms Shortly after onset: cramps around the umbilicus or in the epigastrium, vomiting, and obstipation if the obstruction is complete; partial obstruction may cause diarrhea; severe, steady pain suggests strangulation
claims.quote: Obstruction of the small bowel causes symptoms shortly after onset: abdominal cramps centered around the umbilicus or in the epigastrium, vomiting, and—in patients with complete obstruction—obstipation. Patients with partial obstruction may develop diarrhea. Severe, steady pain suggests that strangulation has occurred.

claims.text: Without strangulation the abdomen is not tender, and hyperactive, high-pitched peristalsis with rushes coinciding with cramps is typical; with infarction it becomes tender with a silent abdomen or minimal peristalsis
claims.quote: In the absence of strangulation, the abdomen is not tender. Hyperactive, high-pitched peristalsis with rushes coinciding with cramps is typical. Sometimes, dilated loops of bowel are palpable. With infarction, the abdomen becomes tender and auscultation reveals a silent abdomen or minimal peristalsis.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: NPO, NGT, IVF; CT to localize transition; surgery if ischemia
claims.quote: NPO, NGT, IVF; CT to localize transition; surgery if ischemia

claims.text: Hospitalize; treatment proceeds alongside diagnosis, and a surgeon should always be involved
claims.quote: Patients with possible intestinal obstruction should be hospitalized. Treatment of acute intestinal obstruction must proceed simultaneously with diagnosis. A surgeon should always be involved.

claims.text: Supportive care: nasogastric suction, IV fluids (0.9% saline or lactated Ringer’s) and a urinary catheter to monitor output
claims.quote: Supportive care is similar for small- and large-bowel obstruction: nasogastric suction, IV fluids (0.9% saline or lactated Ringer’s solution for intravascular volume repletion), and a urinary catheter to monitor fluid output.

claims.text: If ischemia or infarction is suspected: antibiotics (eg, cefotetan or cefoxitin) before operative exploration
claims.quote: If bowel ischemia or infarction is suspected, antibiotics should be given (eg, a third-generation cephalosporin, such as cefotetan or cefoxitin) before operative exploration.

claims.text: Complete SBO: early laparotomy is preferred (it can be delayed 2 or 3 hours to improve fluid status and urine output in a very ill, dehydrated patient)
claims.quote: Complete obstruction of the small bowel is preferentially treated with early laparotomy, although surgery can be delayed 2 or 3 hours to improve fluid status and urine output in a very ill, dehydrated patient.

claims.text: Approximately 85% of partial SBOs resolve with nonoperative treatment; most complete SBOs require surgery
claims.quote: Approximately 85% of partial small-bowel obstructions resolve with nonoperative treatment (1), whereas most complete small-bowel obstructions require surgery.

claims.text: In most patients with early postoperative or repeated adhesive obstruction and no peritoneal signs, nasogastric decompression through a sump tube may be tried; failure to resolve or symptoms or signs of ischemia → surgery
claims.quote: In most patients with early postoperative obstruction or repeated obstruction caused by adhesions, nasogastric decompression through a sump tube may be attempted in the absence of peritoneal signs. Failure of the obstruction to resolve or development of symptoms or signs of ischemia are indications to proceed with surgery.

notes.issue: Merck calls cefotetan/cefoxitin third-generation cephalosporins; they are second-generation (cephamycins), so the site would teach a wrong drug class
notes.resolution: drug class omitted, drugs kept (eg, cefotetan or cefoxitin); re-checked pass
restored 'In most patients' and 'symptoms or signs'; re-checked pass
